_comment: Source registry for restriction_evidence.py.
Registered 2026-09-15. This file answers one question the repository could
not answer before it existed: for a given county, WHAT DID WE CHECK before
recording that it has no enacted data-center restriction?
Until now data/county_aggregate.csv carried 2893 counties labeled
has_enacted_restrictive = 0 and nothing anywhere recorded a single source
consulted for any of them. The label meant 'no row was found', which is a
statement about the tracker, not about the county. Every entry below is a
place a restriction would be visible if it existed, so that a negative can
become a checked claim with a date on it.
INDEPENDENCE CLASSES are the load-bearing idea. Two sources that read the
same underlying material do not corroborate each other: a news-derived
tracker and a second news-derived tracker can be wrong together, and
counting them twice would manufacture confidence the evidence does not
support. Grade A therefore requires agreement across two DISTINCT
independence classes, never two sources within one. The classes are:
primary_law    the adopted instrument itself (county code, ordinance PDF)
proceeding     the record of the body that adopted it (agendas, minutes)
secondary      someone else's compilation (academic census, NGO tracker)
COVERAGE is declared, never assumed. A source that does not publish a
given county is 'not_covered' for that county, which is an honest U grade,
and is never silently treated as a clean check. Absence of coverage and
absence of a restriction are different facts and the grader keeps them
apart.

independence_classes.primary_law: The adopted instrument as published by the adopting jurisdiction.
independence_classes.proceeding: The deliberative record of the adopting body.
independence_classes.secondary: A third-party compilation that read one of the above.

municipal_code.name: Municipal code libraries
why: The strongest available evidence of absence. A county code library
publishes the county's adopted ordinances in full text, so a search
that returns no data-center zoning provision is evidence about the
county rather than about press coverage of the county. This is also
the only family that meaningfully covers zoning_restriction, which is
the most common real-world instrument and the one the external census
barely sees: of 94 census rows, 91 are moratoria and exactly 1 is a
zoning standard.

adapters.name: Municode Library
adapters.notes: Largest US county code host. Jurisdiction list is enumerable per state.

meeting_portal.name: County meeting agendas and minutes
why: Catches an instrument at adoption rather than through later coverage,
which is the detection-bias path the whole platform is built to
reduce. configs/local_meeting_sources.json already holds 848 county
entries, but 557 resolve to platform 'none' and 288 to 'ambiguous',
leaving 3 usable, and its keys are malformed (state prefix empty, e.g.
'::Beaver'). Repairing that registry is tracked as its own task; this
family reads it where it resolves and reports not_covered where it
does not, so a broken registry entry can never read as a clean check.

restriction_census.name: Third-party restriction censuses
why: The family the platform already had, generalized. refresh_external_census.py
reads exactly one upstream; every additional compilation registered here
widens the census past the 17 states and 87 counties it covers today,
against a frame of 3222 counties in which the tracker itself asserts
positives across 43 states. A census is a LOWER BOUND: a county it
lists is a confirmed positive, a county it omits is not a confirmed
negative, so this family can raise a positive grade and can never on
its own clear a county.

adapters.name: Indiana University Environmental Resilience Institute
adapters.notes: Publishes counts without a machine-readable list; rows are hand-seeded into the census.

state_aggregator.name: State-level ordinance and planning repositories
why: Where a state planning agency or AG publishes an ordinance inventory,
it covers every county in the state at once, which is the cheapest
route from grade U to a checked negative across a whole state. Declared
per state because coverage is uneven and asserting national coverage
here would be the exact error this registry exists to prevent.
state_aggregator.notes: Populated per state as repositories are identified and verified. An empty adapter list means this family currently clears no county, which is the honest starting state.

_comment: Pre-registered before any county was graded. The grade answers 'how hard
did we look' for a county recorded as clear, and 'how well corroborated'
for a county recorded as restrictive. It is never a confidence score
about the restriction itself.
grading.A: Two or more distinct independence classes agree, all within the freshness window.
grading.B: One independence class, within the freshness window; or two or more but at least one is stale.
grading.C: Probed, but coverage was partial or a source was unreachable.
grading.D: A registered source family covers this county and it has not been probed yet.
grading.U: No registered source family covers this county. Unverified, and reported as such.

_probe_status: Adapter implementation status, read by restriction_probe.py.
An adapter is run by --backfill only when it carries "implemented": true.
The default is false and that default is load-bearing: an adapter that has
never been written must report not_covered, never clear. A 'clear' from a
stub is indistinguishable from a real check downstream, and it would mark a
county verified that nobody ever read.
All adapters are false as of 2026-09-16. Every probe host below is denied by
the egress policy where this repository's agent sessions run (municode,
amlegal, ecode360, legistar and granicus all answer 403 to CONNECT), so none
could be written and verified against live HTML. A guessed parser is worse
than none: it fails quietly and its result is unattributable.
To implement one: write the probe, verify it against the real site, set
implemented true here, then run restriction_probe.py --backfill. Results
gathered anywhere else can be brought in with --import without touching
